claim: Multisensory integration (MSI) is the process that allows the brain to bind together spatiotemporally congruent inputs from different sensory modalities to produce single salient representations.
source: Multisensory integration (MSI) is the process that allows the brain to bind together spatiotemporally congruent inputs from different sensory modalities to produce single salient representations.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study, but represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: MSI in the Xenopus tadpole optic tectum is highly dependent on the temporal interval between crossmodal stimulus pairs.
source: We find MSI is highly dependent on the temporal interval between crossmodal stimulus pairs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and throughout the results section showing MSI varies with ISI.

claim: Over development (stages 44-46 to 48-49), the temporal window for MSI significantly narrows.
source: Over a key developmental period, the temporal window for MSI significantly narrows and is selectively tuned to specific interstimulus intervals.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2E showing narrower tuning curves in older tadpoles (F-test: F = 9.966 (2716), p<0.00001).

claim: Changes in MSI correlate with developmental increases in evoked synaptic inhibition.
source: These changes in MSI correlate with developmental increases in evoked synaptic inhibition, and inhibitory blockade reverses observed developmental changes in MSI.
evidence: This is supported by voltage clamp data in Figure 7 and pharmacological experiments with picrotoxin in Figure 5.

claim: Inhibitory blockade reverses observed developmental changes in MSI.
source: These changes in MSI correlate with developmental increases in evoked synaptic inhibition, and inhibitory blockade reverses observed developmental changes in MSI.
evidence: This is demonstrated by picrotoxin experiments shown in Figure 5, where blocking inhibition in older tadpoles produces MSI characteristics similar to younger tadpoles.

claim: Development of recurrent inhibition mediates development of temporal aspects of MSI in the tectum.
source: We propose a model in which development of recurrent inhibition mediates development of temporal aspects of MSI in the tectum.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of multiple experimental findings including inhibitory blockade effects and E/I balance measurements.

claim: The optic tectum is a central brain area where inputs from multiple sensory modalities first interact.
source: One central brain area where inputs from multiple sensory modalities first interact is the optic tectum.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations throughout the introduction.

claim: The optic tectum is also known as the superior colliculus in mammals.
source: This midbrain structure, also known as the superior colliculus in mammals, contains laminae that are segregated functionally, as well as anatomically—its superficial layers receive a direct retinal projection that maintains its topographic map of visual space (Graybiel, 1975; Straznicky and Gaze, 1972) and its deep and intermediate layers receive inputs carrying both auditory information (Knudsen, 1982; Lowe, 1986) as well as somato- and mechanosensory information and motor feedback signals (for a review see May, 2006).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The superficial layers of the optic tectum receive a direct retinal projection that maintains its topographic map of visual space.
source: This midbrain structure, also known as the superior colliculus in mammals, contains laminae that are segregated functionally, as well as anatomically—its superficial layers receive a direct retinal projection that maintains its topographic map of visual space (Graybiel, 1975; Straznicky and Gaze, 1972) and its deep and intermediate layers receive inputs carrying both auditory information (Knudsen, 1982; Lowe, 1986) as well as somato- and mechanosensory information and motor feedback signals (for a review see May, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited references (Graybiel, 1975; Straznicky and Gaze, 1972).

claim: The deep and intermediate layers of the optic tectum receive inputs carrying auditory information.
source: This midbrain structure, also known as the superior colliculus in mammals, contains laminae that are segregated functionally, as well as anatomically—its superficial layers receive a direct retinal projection that maintains its topographic map of visual space (Graybiel, 1975; Straznicky and Gaze, 1972) and its deep and intermediate layers receive inputs carrying both auditory information (Knudsen, 1982; Lowe, 1986) as well as somato- and mechanosensory information and motor feedback signals (for a review see May, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited references (Knudsen, 1982; Lowe, 1986).

claim: The deep and intermediate layers of the optic tectum receive somato- and mechanosensory information and motor feedback signals.
source: This midbrain structure, also known as the superior colliculus in mammals, contains laminae that are segregated functionally, as well as anatomically—its superficial layers receive a direct retinal projection that maintains its topographic map of visual space (Graybiel, 1975; Straznicky and Gaze, 1972) and its deep and intermediate layers receive inputs carrying both auditory information (Knudsen, 1982; Lowe, 1986) as well as somato- and mechanosensory information and motor feedback signals (for a review see May, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a review citation (May, 2006).

claim: In multisensory neurons in the colliculus, the amount of integration is dependent on the overlap between spatial receptive fields for the two stimulus modalities.
source: In a given multisensory neuron in the colliculus, the amount of integration is dependent on both the overlap between spatial receptive fields for the two stimulus modalities and the time window between stimulus presentations in a crossmodal pair (Meredith et al., 1987; Meredith and Stein, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by cited references (Meredith et al., 1987; Meredith and Stein, 1996).

claim: In multisensory neurons in the colliculus, the amount of integration is dependent on the time window between stimulus presentations in a crossmodal pair.
source: In a given multisensory neuron in the colliculus, the amount of integration is dependent on both the overlap between spatial receptive fields for the two stimulus modalities and the time window between stimulus presentations in a crossmodal pair (Meredith et al., 1987; Meredith and Stein, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by cited references (Meredith et al., 1987; Meredith and Stein, 1996).

claim: The integrative capabilities of multisensory collicular neurons develop in an activity dependent manner.
source: The integrative capabilities of multisensory collicular neurons develop in an activity dependent manner which has been proposed to depend on repeated associations of spatiotemporally aligned stimuli during a critical period (Knudsen, 2002; Knudsen and Brainard, 1991; Wallace et al., 2006; Wallace and Stein, 2007; Xu et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Development of multisensory integration has been proposed to depend on repeated associations of spatiotemporally aligned stimuli during a critical period.
source: The integrative capabilities of multisensory collicular neurons develop in an activity dependent manner which has been proposed to depend on repeated associations of spatiotemporally aligned stimuli during a critical period (Knudsen, 2002; Knudsen and Brainard, 1991; Wallace et al., 2006; Wallace and Stein, 2007; Xu et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by multiple citations.

claim: Very little experimental work exists on cellular and synaptic mechanisms for multisensory integration and its development.
source: Despite great interest within the field in understanding potential cellular and synaptic mechanisms for multisensory integration and its development (Rowland et al., 2007b), very little experimental work exists on this question (Binns and Salt, 1996; Skaliora et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field supported by limited citations of existing work.

claim: The optic tectum in Xenopus laevis tadpoles is superficially located and accessible for whole-cell recordings in vivo.
source: In Xenopus laevis tadpoles, the optic tectum is superficially located and thus accessible for whole-cell recordings in vivo (Khakhalin et al., 2014) and can be isolated in an intact whole-brain preparation for recordings ex vivo (Pratt and Aizenman, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited references describing the methodology.

claim: The Xenopus tadpole optic tectum can be isolated in an intact whole-brain preparation for recordings ex vivo.
source: In Xenopus laevis tadpoles, the optic tectum is superficially located and thus accessible for whole-cell recordings in vivo (Khakhalin et al., 2014) and can be isolated in an intact whole-brain preparation for recordings ex vivo (Pratt and Aizenman, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference describing the methodology.

claim: In Xenopus, the dominant input to the optic tectum is visual, originating from the contralateral retina.
source: In Xenopus, as in other vertebrates, the dominant input to the optic tectum is visual, originating from the contralateral retina, and terminating in the superficial layers of the tectal neuropil (Deeg et al., 2009; Székely and Lázár, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Visual inputs to the Xenopus optic tectum terminate in the superficial layers of the tectal neuropil.
source: In Xenopus, as in other vertebrates, the dominant input to the optic tectum is visual, originating from the contralateral retina, and terminating in the superficial layers of the tectal neuropil (Deeg et al., 2009; Székely and Lázár, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Inputs from mechanosensory modalities that ascend via hindbrain nuclei terminate within the deeper layers of the Xenopus optic tectum.
source: Inputs from the various mechanosensory modalities that ascend via hindbrain nuclei terminate within the deeper layers (Behrend et al., 2006; Deeg et al., 2009; Hiramoto and Cline, 2009; Lowe, 1986; 1987).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Hindbrain mechanosensory projections to the tectum converge in single tectal neurons from very early developmental stages.
source: Our laboratory and others have characterized the development of hindbrain mechanosensory projections to the tectum in Xenopus tadpoles, and have shown that these inputs converge in single tectal neurons from very early developmental stages.
evidence: This is stated as prior work from the authors' laboratory and others, representing established findings.

claim: Experiments were performed between developmental stages 44–46 and 48–49.
source: Experiments were performed between developmental stages 44–46 and 48–9.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design.

claim: During stages 44-49, tectal neurons have already been innervated by both visual and mechanosensory inputs.
source: During this developmental time span, tectal neurons already have been innervated by both visual and mechanosensory inputs and respond synaptically to activation of either pathway (Deeg et al., 2009; Hiramoto and Cline, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Tectal neurons respond synaptically to activation of either visual or mechanosensory pathways during stages 44-49.
source: During this developmental time span, tectal neurons already have been innervated by both visual and mechanosensory inputs and respond synaptically to activation of either pathway (Deeg et al., 2009; Hiramoto and Cline, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: During stages 44-49, tectal circuits undergo a period of refinement of sensory receptive fields.
source: During this timeframe tectal circuits also undergo a period of refinement, both of sensory receptive fields (Dong and Aizenman, 2012; Dong et al., 2009; Tao and Poo, 2005) and of local recurrent circuitry (Pratt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: During stages 44-49, tectal circuits undergo refinement of local recurrent circuitry.
source: During this timeframe tectal circuits also undergo a period of refinement, both of sensory receptive fields (Dong and Aizenman, 2012; Dong et al., 2009; Tao and Poo, 2005) and of local recurrent circuitry (Pratt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Tectal neurons undergo dramatic change in their intrinsic excitability during stages 44-49.
source: Tectal neurons also undergo dramatic change in their intrinsic excitability (Ciarleglio et al., 2015; Pratt and Aizenman, 2007), and behavioral data demonstrate that even young Xenopus tadpoles generate behavioral responses to visual and mechanosensory stimuli (Dong et al., 2009; Roberts et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Young Xenopus tadpoles generate behavioral responses to visual and mechanosensory stimuli.
source: Tectal neurons also undergo dramatic change in their intrinsic excitability (Ciarleglio et al., 2015; Pratt and Aizenman, 2007), and behavioral data demonstrate that even young Xenopus tadpoles generate behavioral responses to visual and mechanosensory stimuli (Dong et al., 2009; Roberts et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The inter-stimulus interval (ISI) between two crossmodal inputs is a key factor that determines the direction and magnitude of the integrative response.
source: Previous descriptions of crossmodal integration, evidenced in either the number or temporal distribution of action potentials, reveal that the inter-stimulus interval (ISI) between two crossmodal inputs is a key factor that determines the direction and magnitude of the integrative response (Meredith et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Greater multisensory enhancement is observed if the stronger modality precedes the weaker one.
source: This temporal relationship can be further modulated by the relative size of the individual responses, where greater multisensory enhancement is observed if the stronger modality precedes the weaker one (Miller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Paired crossmodal responses have a faster onset than single modality responses.
source: From these examples two observations become evident. First that paired responses have a faster onset and can have a greater gain than single modality responses.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and quantified in Figure 6.

claim: Paired crossmodal responses can have a greater gain than single modality responses.
source: From these examples two observations become evident. First that paired responses have a faster onset and can have a greater gain than single modality responses.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and throughout the results.

claim: Changes in crossmodal responses show a temporal dependence on ISI.
source: And second that these changes show a temporal dependence on ISI.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D showing MSIn varies with ISI.

claim: Greater and more-positive MSIn values were observed as a result of shorter inter-stimulus intervals.
source: In general, greater and more-positive MSIn values were observed as a result of shorter inter-stimulus intervals, whereas negative MSIn values—indicating a suppression of responses due to crossmodal paired stimuli—are produced exclusively by longer inter-stimulus intervals, of up to 1000 ms.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Negative MSIn values indicating suppression of responses are produced exclusively by longer inter-stimulus intervals of up to 1000 ms.
source: In general, greater and more-positive MSIn values were observed as a result of shorter inter-stimulus intervals, whereas negative MSIn values—indicating a suppression of responses due to crossmodal paired stimuli—are produced exclusively by longer inter-stimulus intervals, of up to 1000 ms.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The net average MSIn values appear to be reduced in older animals (stages 48-49 compared to 44-46).
source: Noticeably, the net average MSIn values (both negative and positive) appear to be reduced in the older animals.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figure 1D between the two developmental stages.

claim: In stage 48-49 tadpoles, maximum MSIn responses occur at a relatively broad range of ISIs across the population of cells.
source: We found that in the stage 48–49 group, maximum MSIn responses occur at a relatively broad range of ISIs (Figure 2B) across the population of cells, in contrast to the younger tadpoles, where maximal MSI mostly occurs at short ISIs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In younger tadpoles (stages 44-46), maximal MSI mostly occurs at short ISIs.
source: We found that in the stage 48–49 group, maximum MSIn responses occur at a relatively broad range of ISIs (Figure 2B) across the population of cells, in contrast to the younger tadpoles, where maximal MSI mostly occurs at short ISIs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In older tadpoles (stages 48-49), tectal neurons as a population are tuned to respond optimally to a wider range of crossmodal ISIs compared to younger tadpoles.
source: Another way to describe this is that in the older tadpoles, tectal neurons, as a population, are tuned to respond optimally to a wider range of crossmodal ISIs (Figure 2D; median ISI, st 44–6 = 200 ms, IQR = 300 ms (n=26), st 48–9 = 400 ms, IQR = 775 ms (n=40), p<0.05, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of data shown in Figure 2D (p<0.05, Mann-Whitney test).

claim: The peak MSIn value that could be achieved by a given cell was roughly twice as large in the younger developmental group (stages 44-46) compared to older tadpoles (stages 48-49).
source: However, despite these differences in temporal tuning, the peak MSIn value that could be achieved by a given cell was still roughly twice as large in the younger developmental group (Figure 2C; mean max MSI, st 44–6 = 1.15 ± 0.31 (n=26), st 48–9 = 0.55 ± 0.10 (n=40), p<0.05, unpaired T-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of data shown in Figure 2C (p<0.05, unpaired T-test).

claim: Both H-V and V-H stimulus sequences were equally effective in evoking multisensory responses.
source: Thus we compared the peak MSIn values at the same ISI, across the two stimulus sequences, and consistently we found that both sequences were equally effective in evoking multisensory responses (see Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1 showing no significant differences between presentation orders.

claim: Stage 48-49 cells are more narrowly tuned around their preferred ISI compared to stage 44-46 cells.
source: Stage 48–49 cells are more narrowly tuned around their preferred ISI.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and statistical comparison (F-test: F = 9.966 (2716), p<0.00001).

claim: Over development, peak multisensory responses decrease in terms of absolute gain.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that over development, peak multisensory responses decrease in terms of absolute gain, however cells become preferentially tuned to a greater diversity of temporal intervals, yet also become more sharply tuned around their preferred interval.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data from Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Over development, cells become preferentially tuned to a greater diversity of temporal intervals.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that over development, peak multisensory responses decrease in terms of absolute gain, however cells become preferentially tuned to a greater diversity of temporal intervals, yet also become more sharply tuned around their preferred interval.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data from Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: Over development, cells become more sharply tuned around their preferred interval.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that over development, peak multisensory responses decrease in terms of absolute gain, however cells become preferentially tuned to a greater diversity of temporal intervals, yet also become more sharply tuned around their preferred interval.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data from Figure 2E.

claim: For both developmental stages, data points fall below the line of unity indicating a tendency for sub-linear summation.
source: When we compared the maximal evoked crossmodal response to the response predicted by a linear sum of both inputs, we found that for both developmental stages data points fall below the line of unity indicating a tendency for sub-linear summation (i.e. predicted > actual, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The overall distributions of integrating responses remains stable during the developmental period from stages 44-46 to 48-49.
source: Although the cumulative probability curve shifts towards the right (supralinear) over development (Figure 3C), we found no statistical differences in the distribution of Z scores across developmental groups (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, D = 0.260, p=0.230), indicating that the overall distributions of integrating responses remains stable during this developmental period.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3C (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p=0.230).

claim: The proportion of cells showing sublinear responses decreased and the proportion showing linear responses increased over development.
source: However there was a shift, such that the proportion of cells showing sublinear responses decreased and the proportion showing linear responses increased over development (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Between stages 45 and 49, the temporal dynamics in tectal network activity change, such that evoked recurrent excitation in the tectum decreases and becomes more temporally compact.
source: Between stages 45 and 49, the temporal dynamics in tectal network activity change, such that evoked recurrent excitation in the tectum decreases, and becomes more temporally compact (Pratt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Tectal neurons become less excitable between stages 45 and 49, generating fewer action potentials when depolarized.
source: Furthermore, tectal neurons become less excitable over this developmental time window, generating fewer action potentials when depolarized (Ciarleglio et al., 2015; Pratt and Aizenman, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: At both developmental stages, paired unimodal responses showed significant response enhancement over a wide range of ISIs.
source: We found that at both developmental stages paired unimodal responses showed significant response enhancement over a wide range of ISIs (Figure 4A,B), in contrast to what we had observed for crossmodal responses (Figure 1D, 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: There was significantly more enhancement in response to unimodal pairs than there was for crossmodal pairs.
source: Moreover, there was significantly more enhancement in response to unimodal pairs than there was for crossmodal pairs, and no developmental decrease was observed in the gain of the paired responses (Figure 4C, compare to 2C; mean max PPE, st 44–6 = 2.25 ± 0.44 (n=29), st 48–9 = 2.57 ± 0.33 (n=26), p = 0.56, unpaired T-test).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figure 4C to Figure 2C.

claim: No developmental decrease was observed in the gain of paired unimodal responses.
source: Moreover, there was significantly more enhancement in response to unimodal pairs than there was for crossmodal pairs, and no developmental decrease was observed in the gain of the paired responses (Figure 4C, compare to 2C; mean max PPE, st 44–6 = 2.25 ± 0.44 (n=29), st 48–9 = 2.57 ± 0.33 (n=26), p = 0.56, unpaired T-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 4C (p = 0.56, unpaired T-test).

claim: There was no developmental difference in the range of ISIs that produced the maximal enhancement for unimodal pairs.
source: Similarly, there was also no developmental difference in the range of ISIs that produced the maximal enhancement (Figure 4D, compare to 2D; median ISI, st 44–6 = 400 ms, IQR = 300 ms (n=29), st 48–9 = 400 ms, IQR = 300 ms (n=26, p<0.34, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 4D (p<0.34, Mann-Whitney).

claim: There was no narrowing of the temporal tuning window for unimodal pairs over development.
source: Finally, when we looked at the temporal tuning around the maximal ISI, there was no narrowing of the temporal tuning window for unimodal pairs over development as both tuning curves were not significantly different from each other (Figure 4E, compare to 2E, F = 1.394 (2,544), p = 0.249).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of data shown in Figure 4E (F = 1.394 (2,544), p = 0.249).

claim: At Stage 49, tectal cells can still exhibit robust enhancement to paired stimuli.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that even at Stage 49, tectal cells can still exhibit robust enhancement to paired stimuli, and thus are not constrained by developmental changes in network dynamics and cellular excitability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the unimodal pairing data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Tectal cells at stage 49 are not constrained by developmental changes in network dynamics and cellular excitability.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that even at Stage 49, tectal cells can still exhibit robust enhancement to paired stimuli, and thus are not constrained by developmental changes in network dynamics and cellular excitability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that unimodal pairs still show robust enhancement.

claim: The temporal changes in multisensory integration observed during development likely occur through a different mechanism than general changes in network dynamics and cellular excitability.
source: In light of this observation, the temporal changes in multisensory integration observed during development likely occur through a different mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects on crossmodal vs unimodal pairs.

claim: In the superior colliculus, maturation of inhibitory feedback correlates with the emergence of multisensory integration.
source: In the superior colliculus it has been proposed that maturation of inhibitory feedback correlates with the emergence of multisensory integration.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism in the literature, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: In the tectum, between developmental stages 45 and 49 there is a large increase in evoked inhibitory drive.
source: In the tectum, between developmental stages 45 and 49 there is a large increase in evoked inhibitory drive, as well as a negative shift in the Cl- equilibrium potential (Akerman and Cline, 2006; Miraucourt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Between developmental stages 45 and 49, there is a negative shift in the Cl- equilibrium potential in the tectum.
source: In the tectum, between developmental stages 45 and 49 there is a large increase in evoked inhibitory drive, as well as a negative shift in the Cl- equilibrium potential (Akerman and Cline, 2006; Miraucourt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Inhibition is known to narrow the tuning of sensory neurons to their preferred responses.
source: Inhibition is known to both narrow the tuning of sensory neurons to their preferred responses and to alter the timing and reliability of sensory driven spike output (Shen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Inhibition is known to alter the timing and reliability of sensory driven spike output.
source: Inhibition is known to both narrow the tuning of sensory neurons to their preferred responses and to alter the timing and reliability of sensory driven spike output (Shen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Inhibitory blockade resulted in an overall increase in MSIn values over a wide range of ISIs in stage 48-49 tadpoles.
source: We found that inhibitory blockade resulted in an overall increase in MSIn values over a wide range of ISIs (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Inhibitory blockade caused ISI values at which maximum MSIn was recorded to become shorter and less variable across cells.
source: The ISI values at which the maximum MSIn was recorded were also shorter and became less variable across cells (Figure 5B,D; median ISI, PTX = 100 ms, IQR = 425 ms (n=22), no drug = 400 ms, IQR = 775 ms (n=40), p = 0.029, Mann-Whitney)
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of data shown in Figure 5B and 5D (p = 0.029, Mann-Whitney).

claim: Inhibitory blockade caused the overall maximum MSIn per cell to increase significantly in stage 48-49 tadpoles.
source: and the overall maximum MSIn per cell increased significantly (Figure 5C; mean max MSIn, PTX = 1.96 ± 0.25 (n=22), no drug = 0.55 ± 0.100 (n=40), p = 0.0001, unpaired T-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of data shown in Figure 5C (p = 0.0001, unpaired T-test).

claim: Inhibitory blockade caused a significant broadening of the temporal tuning of the multisensory integration window.
source: Inhibitory blockade also caused a significant broadening of the temporal tuning of the multisensory integration window (Figure 5E, F = 28.72(2678), p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of data shown in Figure 5E (F = 28.72(2678), p<0.0001).

claim: In the presence of picrotoxin, there was an increase in the relative proportion of neurons showing supralinear responses.
source: Inhibitory blockade also affected the linearity of crossmodal responses. In the presence of picrotoxin, there was an increase in the relative proportion of neurons showing supralinear responses (Figure 5F), significantly shifting the cumulative distribution of Z-scores to the right (Figure 5G, D = 0.595, p<0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F and statistical analysis (D = 0.595, p<0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).

claim: Inhibitory blockade did not have any effect on response enhancement caused by unimodal stimulus pairs.
source: Interestingly, inhibitory blockade did not have any effect on response enhancement caused by unimodal stimulus pairs, suggesting that its effects are not due to general enhancement of network excitability (Max PPR, Control: 2.57 ± 0.32, n=26, PTX: 2.17 ± 0.3, n=12, p=0.39; Difference in Z-scores, D=0.267, p=0.413, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparisons (p=0.39 for Max PPR; p=0.413 for Z-scores).

claim: The effects of inhibitory blockade on multisensory integration are not due to general enhancement of network excitability.
source: Interestingly, inhibitory blockade did not have any effect on response enhancement caused by unimodal stimulus pairs, suggesting that its effects are not due to general enhancement of network excitability (Max PPR, Control: 2.57 ± 0.32, n=26, PTX: 2.17 ± 0.3, n=12, p=0.39; Difference in Z-scores, D=0.267, p=0.413, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that unimodal pairs are unaffected by picrotoxin.

claim: In mammals, spiking responses to crossmodal stimulus pairs always have a more rapid onset than responses to single stimuli of either modality.
source: In mammals, spiking responses to crossmodal stimulus pairs always have a more rapid onset, than responses to single stimuli of either modality (Rowland et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: In the Xenopus preparation, paired crossmodal responses are significantly faster than single stimulus responses at both developmental stages.
source: In our preparation we observe the same effect at both developmental stages and across multiple ISIs. Figures 6A and B show the median onset and IQR of spiking responses to both single stimuli and paired stimuli at multiple ISIs for all cells, and we consistently find that paired crossmodal responses are significantly faster than single stimulus responses (Figure 6D; st 44–6: p<0.0001, n=25, st 48–49: p=0.04, n= 36, PTX: p<0.0001, n=19, paired T-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparisons shown in Figure 6D (p<0.0001 for st 44-6; p=0.04 for st 48-49).

claim: In picrotoxin, paired responses still have a faster onset than single responses.
source: We find that in picrotoxin, while paired responses still have a faster onset than single responses (Figure 6C,D), the onset of paired responses is significantly delayed when compared to stage 48–9 controls (Figure 6E; p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: In picrotoxin, the onset of paired responses is significantly delayed when compared to stage 48-9 controls.
source: We find that in picrotoxin, while paired responses still have a faster onset than single responses (Figure 6C,D), the onset of paired responses is significantly delayed when compared to stage 48–9 controls (Figure 6E; p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 6E (p<0.05).

claim: Inhibition regulates the temporal tuning and gain of multisensory integration.
source: This suggests that inhibition not only regulates the temporal tuning and gain of multisensory integration, but also regulates the timing of tectal cell output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of picrotoxin on MSI properties shown in Figure 5.

claim: Inhibition regulates the timing of tectal cell output.
source: This suggests that inhibition not only regulates the temporal tuning and gain of multisensory integration, but also regulates the timing of tectal cell output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of picrotoxin on response onset shown in Figure 6.

claim: Inhibitory conductances were much greater in general than excitatory conductances.
source: Overall, we found that inhibitory conductances were much greater in general than excitatory conductances and that the ratio of excitation to inhibition varied greatly across cells, consistent with prior observations (Akerman and Cline, 2006; Khakhalin and Aizenman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and cited references.

claim: The ratio of excitation to inhibition varied greatly across cells.
source: Overall, we found that inhibitory conductances were much greater in general than excitatory conductances and that the ratio of excitation to inhibition varied greatly across cells, consistent with prior observations (Akerman and Cline, 2006; Khakhalin and Aizenman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and cited references.

claim: At both developmental stages there was an overall enhancement of both excitatory and inhibitory multisensory responses across all ISIs.
source: At both developmental stages we found on average an overall enhancement of both excitatory and inhibitory multisensory responses across all ISIs (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: There was proportionally greater enhancement across ISIs of excitatory responses in stage 44-46 tadpoles compared to stage 48-49.
source: However we found proportionally greater enhancement across ISIs of excitatory responses in the stage 44–46 tadpoles, compared to stage 48–49 (p=0.037, 2-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of data shown in Figure 7B (p=0.037, 2-way ANOVA).

claim: Enhancement of inhibitory conductances and its dependence on ISI did not change over the developmental time window from stages 44-46 to 48-49.
source: In contrast we found that enhancement of inhibitory conductances, and its dependence on ISI, did not change over this developmental time window.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Maximal Excitatory and Inhibitory MSIn values were positively correlated in both developmental stages.
source: We also compared data from individual cells by plotting the maximal Excitatory MSIn vs. the corresponding Inhibitory MSIn for both developmental stages (Figure 7D). In both cases maximal Excitatory and Inhibitory MSIn values were positively correlated (St 44–46: r = 0.758, p<0.0001; St 48–49: r=0.767, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The ratio between excitatory enhancement and inhibitory enhancement was greater in younger tadpoles than in older tadpoles.
source: However the ratio between excitatory enhancement and inhibitory enhancement was greater in younger tadpoles than in older tadpoles, overall, consistent with the observation that excitatory currents show proportionally greater MSIn values than inhibitory currents (test for differences in slopes of linear fits: p=0.023, F = 5.56(1,45).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of slopes shown in Figure 7D (p=0.023, F = 5.56(1,45)).

claim: In younger tadpoles, the ratio of excitation to inhibition in response to crossmodal stimulus is greater than in the older group.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that in younger tadpoles, the ratio of excitation to inhibition, in response to crossmodal stimulus, is greater than in the older group, which may in part explain the greater amount of multisensory enhancement of spike output observed in the younger tadpoles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The change in the excitation to inhibition ratio may explain the sharpening of the temporal tuning of multisensory responses.
source: This change in the excitation to inhibition ratio may also explain the sharpening of the temporal tuning of multisensory responses.
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting the E/I balance data to the temporal tuning observations.

claim: Crossmodal inputs to the tectum recruit local networks of excitatory neurons, resulting in enhanced tectal cell responses.
source: Taken together our data are consistent with a model in which crossmodal inputs to the tectum recruit local networks of excitatory neurons, resulting in enhanced tectal cell responses.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of experimental findings.

claim: Crossmodal inputs recruit local inhibition.
source: Crossmodal inputs also recruit local inhibition, and the relative enhancement of inhibition, versus excitation, increases over development.
evidence: This is supported by the voltage clamp data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The relative enhancement of inhibition versus excitation increases over development.
source: Crossmodal inputs also recruit local inhibition, and the relative enhancement of inhibition, versus excitation, increases over development.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: The change in relative enhancement of inhibition versus excitation sculpts the temporal sensitivity of the tectal network such that individual neurons become more narrowly tuned to specific ISIs.
source: This change in relative enhancement sculpts the temporal sensitivity of the tectal network such that individual neurons become more narrowly tuned to specific ISIs, thus enhancing the diversity of responses to different temporal combinations of inputs.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on integration of multiple experimental findings.

claim: Local inhibition serves to constrain the timing of evoked multisensory responses by limiting the temporal window in which spikes can occur during a response.
source: Local inhibition also serves to constrain the timing of evoked multisensory responses, by limiting the temporal window in which spikes can occur during a response, and thus shortening response latencies.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the picrotoxin effects on response timing shown in Figure 6.

claim: The inhibition to excitation ratio can sharpen the tuning of sensory neurons to their preferred stimulus.
source: There is ample evidence throughout the nervous system that suggests that the inhibition to excitation ratio can sharpen the tuning of sensory neurons to their preferred stimulus (Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Priebe and Ferster, 2008; Shen et al., 2011; Wehr and Zador, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Having more inhibition can limit the range of stimuli that can effectively drive a cell above spike threshold.
source: Having more inhibition can limit the range of stimuli that can effectively drive a cell above spike threshold.
evidence: This is a general principle of neuronal function based on established knowledge.

claim: Inhibitory feedback has been proposed to be a central mechanism for regulating multisensory integration in the superior colliculus.
source: Although inhibitory feedback has been proposed to be a central mechanism for regulating multisensory integration in the superior colliculus (Rowland et al., 2007b), to our knowledge ours is the first experimental evidence directly supporting this model.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism in the literature supported by a citation.

claim: This study provides the first experimental evidence directly supporting the model that inhibitory feedback regulates multisensory integration.
source: Although inhibitory feedback has been proposed to be a central mechanism for regulating multisensory integration in the superior colliculus (Rowland et al., 2007b), to our knowledge ours is the first experimental evidence directly supporting this model.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current findings.

claim: The temporal tuning of crossmodal responses can be strongly dependent on input size disparity.
source: Recent work by Miller et al. (2015) shows that the temporal tuning of crossmodal responses can be strongly dependent on input size disparity, such that if the stronger modality is presented first, there will be a greater amount of multisensory enhancement than if the weaker modality is presented first.
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: When both modalities are matched in their response sizes, the temporal order becomes less important.
source: When both modalities are matched in their response sizes, then the temporal order becomes less important.
evidence: This is based on cited work by Miller et al. (2015).

claim: The 'stronger-first' rule is thought to result from differential recruitment of inhibition.
source: This 'stronger-first' rule is thought to result from differential recruitment of inhibition.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from the literature.

claim: In the superior colliculus of mammals, there are clear demonstrations of dependency of multisensory integration to the temporal interval between different modality inputs.
source: Our findings in the optic tectum also share other fundamental similarities and differences with other animal models of multisensory integration. (i) In the superior colliculus of mammals (Meredith et al., 1987) as well as in the optic tectum of owls (Bergan and Knudsen, 2009), there are clear demonstrations of dependency of multisensory integration to the temporal interval between different modality inputs.
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: In the optic tectum of owls, there are clear demonstrations of dependency of multisensory integration to the temporal interval between different modality inputs.
source: Our findings in the optic tectum also share other fundamental similarities and differences with other animal models of multisensory integration. (i) In the superior colliculus of mammals (Meredith et al., 1987) as well as in the optic tectum of owls (Bergan and Knudsen, 2009), there are clear demonstrations of dependency of multisensory integration to the temporal interval between different modality inputs.
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: A developmental narrowing of the temporal window underlying multisensory integration has been shown behaviorally in humans.
source: Furthermore, a developmental narrowing of the temporal window underlying multisensory integration has been shown behaviorally in humans (Hillock et al., 2011) and has been proposed to mediate development of important cognitive processes such as temporal binding.
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Developmental narrowing of the temporal window for multisensory integration has been proposed to mediate development of important cognitive processes such as temporal binding.
source: Furthermore, a developmental narrowing of the temporal window underlying multisensory integration has been shown behaviorally in humans (Hillock et al., 2011) and has been proposed to mediate development of important cognitive processes such as temporal binding.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism in the literature.

claim: In mammals, collicular cells show differences in the type of integration, having a combination of supralinear, linear and sublinear responses.
source: (ii) Second, like in the tadpole tectum, in mammals, collicular cells show also differences in the type of integration, having a combination of supralinear, linear and sublinear responses (Alvarado et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: An important aspect that underlies the development of multisensory integration in the mammalian colliculus is the presence of cortical feedback.
source: (iii) Third, another important aspect that underlies the development of multisensory integration in the mammalian colliculus is the presence of cortical feedback (Jiang et al., 2001; Wallace et al., 1993; Wallace and Stein, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: During the developmental stages used in this study, tadpoles have forebrain feedback into the tectum.
source: While tadpoles do not have a proper cortex, during the developmental stages used in this study tadpoles do have forebrain feedback into the tectum (Zittlau et al., 1988), as well a local recurrent circuits (Pratt et al., 2008) which can provide the necessary excitatory network activity to drive multisensory integration in individual neurons.
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Tadpoles have local recurrent circuits which can provide the necessary excitatory network activity to drive multisensory integration in individual neurons.
source: While tadpoles do not have a proper cortex, during the developmental stages used in this study tadpoles do have forebrain feedback into the tectum (Zittlau et al., 1988), as well a local recurrent circuits (Pratt et al., 2008) which can provide the necessary excitatory network activity to drive multisensory integration in individual neurons.
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference and represents an inference about function.

claim: Based on the timing of tectal neuron spiking, it is likely that recurrent activity drives the majority of spiking activity, rather than the afferent input itself.
source: The relative contributions of both of these feedback circuits on multisensory integration remains to be determined, yet based on the timing of the tectal neuron spiking, it is likely that it is this recurrent activity that drives the majority of spiking activity, rather than the afferent input itself (Pratt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on timing data and supported by a citation.

claim: The temporal output characteristics of recurrent circuits in the tectum have been shown to be highly plastic in response to experience.
source: Since the temporal output characteristics of these recurrent circuits has been shown to be highly plastic in response to experience (Pratt et al., 2008), this raises the possibility that this network plasticity can help tune the selectivity of different tectal cells over development to specific combinations of crossmodal ISIs.
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Network plasticity can help tune the selectivity of different tectal cells over development to specific combinations of crossmodal ISIs.
source: Since the temporal output characteristics of these recurrent circuits has been shown to be highly plastic in response to experience (Pratt et al., 2008), this raises the possibility that this network plasticity can help tune the selectivity of different tectal cells over development to specific combinations of crossmodal ISIs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on known plasticity properties.

claim: In the mammalian superior colliculus, temporal statistics of cross-modal stimuli during development and in adulthood shape the temporal tuning of multisensory responses.
source: This type of network plasticity may also help explain observations in the mammalian superior colliculus where temporal statistics of cross-modal stimuli during development and in adulthood shape the temporal tuning of multisensory responses (Xu et al., 2012: Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Pairs of unimodal stimuli result in greater integration over a wider range of intervals than crossmodal pairs in the present study.
source: Our findings also show some important differences with the mammalian literature. (i) In the present study we find that pairs of unimodal stimuli result in greater integration over a wider range of intervals than crossmodal pairs.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing Figure 4 to Figures 1 and 2.

claim: In mammals, crossmodal inputs are more effective than unimodal ones.
source: This finding is opposite to what is observed in mammals, where crossmodal inputs are more effective than unimodal ones (Alvarado et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: One mechanism underlying the difference between tadpole and mammalian MSI is due to presynaptic interactions that lead to paired pulse facilitation.
source: There are likely two mechanisms underlying this difference. The first is due to presynaptic interactions that lead to paired pulse facilitation, which has been described for both visual and hindbrain inputs in the tadpole tectum (Deeg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by a citation.

claim: Paired pulse facilitation has been described for both visual and hindbrain inputs in the tadpole tectum.
source: There are likely two mechanisms underlying this difference. The first is due to presynaptic interactions that lead to paired pulse facilitation, which has been described for both visual and hindbrain inputs in the tadpole tectum (Deeg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: A second mechanism for greater unimodal integration may be due to localization of inputs in the dendritic arbor of tectal neurons.
source: The second may be due to localization of inputs in the dendritic arbor of tectal neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about mechanism.

claim: Unisensory pairs might be more effective in driving local dendritic depolarization since they are not spatially segregated.
source: Unisensory pairs thus, might be more effective in driving local dendritic depolarization since they are not spatially segregated, and therefore activate non linear response elements such as NMDA receptors or voltage gate Ca++ channels, thus enhancing the amount of integration.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: The developmental decrease in pair-driven enhancement of excitatory conductances and spike output appears to contradict developmental studies in mammals.
source: (ii) A second key difference is that the developmental decrease in pair-driven enhancement of excitatory conductances and spike output appears to contradict developmental studies in mammals, where the progressive refinement of superior colliculus receptive fields is associated with the capacity for response enhancement, after paired stimulation (Wallace and Stein, 1997).
evidence: This is a comparison to cited literature.

claim: In mammals, the progressive refinement of superior colliculus receptive fields is associated with the capacity for response enhancement after paired stimulation.
source: (ii) A second key difference is that the developmental decrease in pair-driven enhancement of excitatory conductances and spike output appears to contradict developmental studies in mammals, where the progressive refinement of superior colliculus receptive fields is associated with the capacity for response enhancement, after paired stimulation (Wallace and Stein, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: An analogous developmental refinement of visually-driven receptive fields is found for both excitatory and inhibitory conductances in the X. laevis optic tectum over stages 44-49.
source: Indeed, an analogous developmental refinement of visually-driven receptive fields, specifically, is found for both excitatory and inhibitory conductances—recorded in the same neuron—in the X. laevis optic tectum over the same developmental stages examined here (Tao and Poo, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: The use of bipolar stimulating electrodes has no selectivity for spatiotopic organization.
source: One possible explanation for this discrepancy is the use of bipolar stimulating electrodes in our preparation to evoke action potentials throughout an afferent pathway. While this stimulation paradigm provides excellent temporal control of stimulus delivery, this stimulation method by its nature has no selectivity for spatiotopic organization.
evidence: This is a methodological limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Each electrical stimulus is considered 'whole-field' and loses its spatial specificity.
source: Each stimulus is therefore considered 'whole-field', and loses its spatial specificity.
evidence: This is a characterization of the experimental approach.

claim: In vivo stimuli are likely to have more temporally complex patterns that may result in somewhat different multisensory interactions.
source: Furthermore, in vivo stimuli are likely to also have more temporally complex patterns that may result in somewhat different multisensory interactions.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential differences between the experimental preparation and natural conditions.

claim: In tadpoles, tectal neurons are innervated by sensory input from very early developmental stages.
source: A second possible explanation to this discrepancy between tadpole tectum and mammalian colliculus, is that in tadpoles tectal neurons are innervated by sensory input from very early developmental stages (Gaze et al., 1974), and thus the developmental stages of the circuits in this study may correspond to a much younger stage than what is typically looked at in mammalian studies.
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: The developmental stages of the circuits in this study may correspond to a much younger stage than what is typically looked at in mammalian studies.
source: A second possible explanation to this discrepancy between tadpole tectum and mammalian colliculus, is that in tadpoles tectal neurons are innervated by sensory input from very early developmental stages (Gaze et al., 1974), and thus the developmental stages of the circuits in this study may correspond to a much younger stage than what is typically looked at in mammalian studies.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed differences.

claim: Some of the basic features and computations of multisensory integration observed in higher order mammalian preparations are conserved in the developing amphibian tectum.
source: We have also shown that some of the basic features and computations of multisensory integration observed in higher order mammalian preparations are conserved in the developing amphibian tectum, indicating that these are likely to be fundamental and evolutionarily conserved processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarities observed between tadpole and mammalian systems.

claim: The basic features and computations of multisensory integration are likely to be fundamental and evolutionarily conserved processes.
source: We have also shown that some of the basic features and computations of multisensory integration observed in higher order mammalian preparations are conserved in the developing amphibian tectum, indicating that these are likely to be fundamental and evolutionarily conserved processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on conservation across species.

claim: Several neurodevelopmental disorders including autism are often accompanied with deficits in sensory integration.
source: Several neurodevelopmental disorders including autism, are often accompanied with deficits in sensory integration (Baum et al., 2015; Markram and Markram, 2010; Foxe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Wild-type Xenopus laevis tadpoles reach developmental stages 44-46 at 7-10 dpf.
source: In our laboratory, tadpoles reach the Nieuwkoop and Faber (Nieuwkoop and Faber, 1956) developmental stages 44–46 at 7–10 dpf, and stage 48–49 at 14 dpf.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental animals used.

claim: Wild-type Xenopus laevis tadpoles reach stage 48-49 at 14 dpf.
source: In our laboratory, tadpoles reach the Nieuwkoop and Faber (Nieuwkoop and Faber, 1956) developmental stages 44–46 at 7–10 dpf, and stage 48–49 at 14 dpf.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental animals used.

claim: The reversal potential of excitatory AMPA and NMDA receptor-mediated currents is +5 mV.
source: Previous work in the laboratory has shown that the reversal potential of excitatory AMPA and NMDA receptor-mediated currents is +5 mV and the reversal potential of synaptic currents mediated by inhibitory GABAA receptors is –45 mV (Bell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference from prior work.

claim: The reversal potential of synaptic currents mediated by inhibitory GABAA receptors is -45 mV.
source: Previous work in the laboratory has shown that the reversal potential of excitatory AMPA and NMDA receptor-mediated currents is +5 mV and the reversal potential of synaptic currents mediated by inhibitory GABAA receptors is –45 mV (Bell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference from prior work.
